https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c52e.text: Image source, Owen Ndlovu/Facebook Image caption, Owen Ndlovu was a familiar face to South African sports audiences after years as an SABC presenter By Wycliffe Muia Published 17 September 2026, 07:46 BST Tributes are pouring in for a veteran South African sports broadcaster who was found dead on Wednesday hours after being abducted when his vehicle was hijacked in a township near Johannesburg. Owen Ndlovu, a former presenter with the country's public broadcaster, the SABC, was seized on Tuesday while collecting his wife from a church in Katlehong, police said. His body, which witnesses said had gunshot wounds, was discovered by residents the following morning. Police have launched a manhunt for three suspects and are investigating the circumstances surrounding his killing, which has once again drawn attention to South Africa's high levels of violent crime. South African president vows justice as more women's bodies found near Johannesburg Published 1 day ago South Africa's deadly love affair with guns Published 23 March 2024 Provincial police spokesperson Col Dimakatso Nevhuhulwi said Ndlovu had gone to pick up his wife from a religious service when the attackers struck. "As she approached their vehicle, three unknown men, one reportedly armed with a firearm, suddenly approached them, pushed her aside and forced her husband into the back seat," she said. "The suspects then drove off with the victim." The vehicle, a Ford Raptor pick-up truck - commonly known as a bakkie in South Africa - was later recovered abandoned in Walkerville, an area south of Johannesburg, police said. Ndlovu's body was found by local residents beside a road in Thokoza, which neighbours Katlehong. They said he appeared to have suffered gunshot wounds. A bag of his was found a few metres away. Police said they were investigating a case of murder but a post-mortem examination would establish the cause of death. "At this stage, the family is awaiting further information from the relevant authorities regarding the circumstances surrounding Owen's death," said family spokesperson Eugene Mthethwa. The family described the loss as "devastating" and thanked residents, police and members of the public who had helped search for him after news of his abduction emerged. Ndlovu was a familiar figure to South African sports fans after years working as a presenter and producer at the SABC. He was also involved in radio coverage of the country's Premier Soccer League and later became an advocate for musicians' rights and royalty payments. The 54-year-old was also associated with Artists United and the SABC Summer Song of the Year initiative. Lelo Mzaca, a fellow journalist, remembered him as a man who lived a "colourful, energetic life" and brought enthusiasm and flair to sports broadcasting. "South Africa has lost a unique and spirited individual whose light shone brightly while it lasted," Mzaca added in a tribute on the Mail & Guardian news site. The provincial government urged communities to help police with the investigation, saying tackling crime remained a priority. The killing has again drawn attention to violent crime in South Africa, where armed robberies and vehicle hijackings remain a major concern. The latest national police figures, covering April to June 2026, recorded more than 5,000 murders and close to 4,000 carjackings. When releasing the figures last month, acting Police Minister Firoz Cachalia said serious crimes continued to create fear in communities and that some were carried out by "organised, heavily armed criminal groups that operate with planning and sophistication". https://www.politico.eu/article/trump-sa.text: BRUSSELS — The G7 group of rich countries has agreed to release 100 million barrels of oil over the next four months, following intense pressure from the Trump administration for Europe to tap its stockpiles of diesel. In a joint statement following an emergency meeting on Friday, the G7 leaders said the release of 100 million barrels of oil would "begin immediately" and would start with release of diesel stocks. The announcement comes after POLITICO reported earlier this week that the U.S. administration had requested European countries to release reserves of diesel into the market to cushion a sharp rise in prices of the fuel, which was becoming a political problem for the Republicans ahead of next month's midterm elections. Advertisement Advertisement Trump had also threatened to ban exports of diesel altogether — a major worry for European countries because U.S. diesel accounts for more than half of the continent's imports of the fuel. But that threat is now off the table, G7 leaders said Friday. Under the agreement there would be "no restrictions or bans on exports among G7 countries," the statement read. French President Emmanuel Macron denied European leaders had been strong-armed into making the concession with the threat of a diesel export, telling press on Friday: "The tone of our discussion was not one of threats; it was constructive." He added that Trump had been "very clear" that there would be no export ban. The leaders' statement did not specify that the releases would come from European reserves, but U.S. President Donald Trump said in a social media post that European countries had agreed to make a major contribution. "Europe has just agreed to release a massive amount of their heavily stocked Diesel Oil," Trump wrote on Truth Social. "The process will begin immediately." Advertisement Advertisement The announcement comes after several rounds of emergency talks between European governments over how to respond to the U.S. pressure, with France proposing a release of 100 million barrels of European oil and diesel earlier Friday. The G7 includes Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, the U.K. and the U.S. While G7 countries participated in a release of 400 million barrels of oil earlier this year led by the International Energy Agency, many of the barrels released never made it to market because they were unable to compete with cheaper U.S. crude that has recently flooded the bloc, according to a trader and an EU diplomat. But they were, officially, available, the people said. Two other diplomats suggested Friday that the announcement was simply a reaffirmation of that March commitment.

More than 70 companies from 17 countries, along with observers from NATO countries, including Slovakia, Latvia and the USA, are participating in the third edition of the Drone Shield 2026 exercise. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6re.text: Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Shamonda virus mostly affects livestock, in whom it can cause fever, diarrhoea and poor milk production By Maia Davies Â and Â Michelle Roberts ,Â digital health editor Published 22 October 2026, 12:04 BST Updated 7 hours ago The first known human case of the Shamonda virus (Shav) has been detected in a patient who died in early October, French authorities have said. Health officials said it was an "exceptional case in a severely immunocompromised patient" and there was currently no risk to the public. Shav is a disease that primarily affects cattle and can be spread by infected midges. Cases have also occurred in sheep, goats, alpacas and horses, but infections in people were previously unheard of. The World Health Organization (WHO) and European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC) said they were monitoring the situation, with French officials still investigating how the virus had spread to a human. It is currently thought the patient contracted Shav through a midge bite in eastern France, the country's health and agriculture ministries said on Thursday, where cases were first identified in animals in the spring. They said the patient was being treated for a serious illness in a Lyon hospital and experienced neurological complications thought to have been "very likely linked" to the virus, based on initial findings. The statement stressed that their immune system was weakened, leaving them more vulnerable to getting ill. "Until now, the Shamonda virus was considered non-transmissible to humans," it noted, having only been identified in animals "despite decades of circulation of the Shamonda virus in Africa and Asia". Dairy herds that catch Shav from bites can experience fever, diarrhoea and poor milk production. The WHO confirmed this was the first documented human case of the disease. It said it had not yet made its own formal risk assessment, but advised that current information and knowledge of similar diseases suggested the case was isolated and "unlikely to lead to wider spread at this time". "Transmissibility of midge-borne viruses also generally declines during the cooler months of the year," it added in a statement. The ECDC said it was working with French and European partners to investigate the "potential public health implications" of the infection. The first cases of the virus in Europe were identified in late July, the agency said. It has since been detected in farm animals in several countries, including Ireland, Germany, Italy and Spain, as well as in Jersey. Photograph: Zeynep Demir Aslim/Zuma Press Wire/Shutterstock View image in fullscreen Farage said at a press conference in Westminster that he had decided to give parliament a ‘wide berth’ on budget day. Photograph: Zeynep Demir Aslim/Zuma Press Wire/Shutterstock Budget 2026 Nigel Farage skips budget in Commons over seating ‘altercation’ concerns Reform UK leader ‘shocked’ by £10bn pledged to Ukraine and doubles down on cutting tax for crypto investors Budget 2026: key points at a glance Rowena Mason Whitehall editor Wed 28 Oct 2026 15.42 EDT First published on Wed 28 Oct 2026 14.21 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Nigel Farage skipped the chancellor’s first budget because he was worried he would get in a “physical altercation” with another MP in a row over seating arrangements. The Reform UK leader was not present in the House of Commons but gave a press conference afterwards in which he said he was “shocked” by the £10bn going to support Ukraine and doubled down on his party’s policies on cutting tax for crypto investors. In a joint event with Robert Jenrick, his party’s Treasury spokesperson, Farage said he had decided to give parliament a “wide berth” as he was concerned he would get into a fight because another MP had removed a green paper slip saving him a seat. He said this situation had turned physical on a previous occasion. “At the state opening of parliament, I got involved in, I didn’t want to, but I got involved in a physical altercation with an MP in the chamber,” he said. “I didn’t make a fuss about it. I didn’t complain. But I could see, given that my prayer card had been removed, I was heading towards another physical altercation, and just sometimes, it’s better to avoid conflict, is one reason. Second reason is, actually, I sat going through the budget with the economists in the office line by line.” It later emerged that the seat reservation was removed for not being properly stamped with the date. A House of Commons spokesperson said: “There are clear and long-established arrangements for members to reserve their own seats in the chamber using prayer cards displaying a valid date stamp. Today, a prayer card placed on a seat did not display a valid date stamp and was removed in line with the usual chamber protocol.” In his response to the budget, Farage said John Healey’s small giveaways suggested there would be a general election in May next year and added that Reform would be ready for one as early as December. Farage criticised the extra taxation announced on gambling shops through higher machine-games duty, saying it would be bad for the horse-racing industry and drive gambling offshore and through crypto. Asked whether Reform still had a policy of cutting capital gains tax on cryptocurrency, which could benefit its big donors, Farage said his plans still stood and would not benefit his backers overall. He said his policy was trying to “bring crypto in from the cold … A 10% tax rate on crypto gains is a way of incentivising people to come into the system, to go straight in a new regulated industry.” On Ukraine , Farage said he was “surprised by the amount” of promised economic and military aid but that he did not “mind the amount, provided I can be absolutely assured it’s not going to get swallowed up in corruption and making Ukrainian officials richer than they already are”. He claimed to be more worried about Vladimir Putin’s “rationality” than at any point before in the conflict, but said he was “shocked by the size of [the aid package]” and was “really concerned the money’s going to get used properly and spent well”. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to First Edition Our morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it matters after newsletter promotion Budget winners and losers: pensioners and households gain as banks and betting shops hit Read more Farage has previously expressed admiration for the Russian president and in 2024 suggested the west “provoked” Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, although he has supported the UK’s position in the war and declined to repeat Donald Trump’s harsher criticisms of Kyiv. Asked whether he preferred Healey’s budget or the disastrous one given under Liz Truss in 2022, which he previously praised but led to Truss’s demise as prime minister, Farage said he had liked the top lines of the Truss budget but “what I hadn’t understood was they didn’t cut spending”. He added: “That was their mistake … If they cut spending radically, they could have cut taxes, and that was the big lesson that came from it.” The Reform leader also gave his response to Tommy Robinson’s conviction for harassing journalists, saying the far-right agitator’s behaviour had obviously been “very wrong”. But he repeated suggestions that his party’s members would not be penalised for admiring Robinson, saying just because they liked a social media message “doesn’t make them full-blown marchers in support of their cause”.
